question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

We went to the mall; however, us only gone window-shopping.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. we only went.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined part "us only gone" has two errors:

◦ "us" is an objective-case pronoun and cannot work as the subject of a clause; the subject form "we" is required.

◦ "gone" is the past participle (V3) and cannot stand alone as a finite verb; it needs an auxiliary (has/had gone). Since the first clause is in the simple past ("We went to the mall"), the second clause must also be simple past — "went".

• Hence "us only gone" must be replaced by "we only went".

◦ Correct: We went to the mall; however, we only went window-shopping.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "No improvement" is wrong because the sentence as printed is ungrammatical on both counts above.

• Option 3 "they only going" changes the doer (the subject is "we", not "they") and uses the bare "-ing" form without an auxiliary.

• Option 4 "we only gone" fixes only the pronoun; "gone" still has no helping verb.

NOTE

• Subject pronouns: I, we, you, he, she, it, they. Object pronouns: me, us, you, him, her, it, them.

• Verb forms of "go": go (V1) – went (V2) – gone (V3). V3 is used only with have/has/had/be: "we have gone", never "we gone".

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

Make sure you known how to swim.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. you known.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Known" is the past participle (V3) of "know" and cannot be used as the finite verb of the clause without an auxiliary. After the subject "you", the simple present form "know" is required.

◦ Correct: Make sure you know how to swim.

• The imperative "Make sure" is followed by a noun clause ("(that) you know how to swim"), whose verb must agree with its own subject "you" — hence "know".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "Make sure" (Option 3) is a correct imperative expression meaning "ensure".

• "how to swim." (Option 2) is a correct infinitive after a wh-word structure (how + to + V1).

• Since a clear error exists, Option 1 "No error" cannot be selected.

NOTE

• Verb forms of "know": know (V1) – knew (V2) – known (V3). V3 appears only with have/has/had or be: "I have known him for years", "It is known to all".

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

“May I ______ your coats, Mr. and Mrs. Mason?”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. take.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Take" here means to receive something from somebody in order to look after it. Offering to "take someone's coat" is the standard polite expression used by a host or attendant when a guest arrives. (लेना / संभालना)

◦ Correct: “May I take your coats, Mr. and Mrs. Mason?”

• "May I ..." is a polite request/offer structure and is always followed by the base form (V1) of the verb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "taste" means to sample the flavour of food — it cannot apply to coats.

• Option 3 "trek" means to make a long, difficult journey on foot (an intransitive verb of travel).

• Option 4 "track" means to follow the trail of a person or animal — it does not fit an offer of hospitality.

NOTE

• Common hospitality collocations: "take your coat", "show you in", "offer you a drink", "make yourself at home".

• After modal verbs (may, can, could, shall, will, must) always use the bare infinitive: may take, can go, must see.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym to substitute the bracketed word in the given sentence.

They wanted me to (expound) on this topic because I had some decent ideas on the subject.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. expatiate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Expound" means to explain something in detail; to set out an idea at length. Its closest synonym is "expatiate", which means to speak or write at length/in detail on a subject. (विस्तार से समझाना)

◦ Correct: They wanted me to expatiate on this topic because I had some decent ideas on the subject.

• Both verbs are typically followed by the preposition "on/upon": "expound on a theory", "expatiate upon a theme" — which is exactly the structure of the given sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "paucity" is a noun meaning scarcity or a very small amount (कमी) — it is not even the same part of speech.

• Option 2 "notoriety" is a noun meaning fame for something bad (कुख्याति).

• Option 3 "partisan" is a noun/adjective meaning a strong, biased supporter of a party or cause (पक्षपाती).

NOTE

• Synonyms of expound/expatiate: elaborate, elucidate, explicate, enlarge upon, dwell on.

• Antonyms: abridge, condense, summarise, curtail.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

The front part is used for carving / the lines and the back end / for scratching of whole areas.
option_1: the lines and the back end
option_3: The front part is used for carving
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. for scratching of whole areas.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The gerund "scratching" is used here as a verb form taking a direct object, so it must be followed directly by its object — the preposition "of" is superfluous.

◦ Correct: The front part is used for carving the lines and the back end for scratching whole areas.

• Compare the parallel first half of the sentence: "used for carving the lines" — no "of" is used there either. Grammatical parallelism therefore also demands "for scratching whole areas".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "The front part is used for carving" is correct — "be used for + V-ing" is the standard pattern for stating purpose.

• Option 1 "the lines and the back end" is correct; it simply completes the first clause and introduces the second subject.

• Option 2 "No Error" cannot be chosen because a clear redundancy exists in the last segment.

NOTE

• A gerund keeps its verbal force: it takes an object directly (writing letters, scratching areas). Adding "of" turns it into a noun-like structure that then needs an article — "the scratching of whole areas" — which does not fit "used for".

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

Break sweat
option_3: To use a lot of energy or effort
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To use a lot of energy or effort.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "break (a) sweat" means to exert oneself; to work hard enough to perspire, i.e., to use a lot of energy or effort. (कड़ी मेहनत करना / जोर लगाना)

◦ Example: He finished the whole job without breaking a sweat, so easy was it for him.

• The image behind the idiom is physical: real effort makes a person sweat, so "breaking a sweat" = putting in genuine effort.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "To make a futile attempt" matches idioms like "flog a dead horse" or "beat the air".

• Option 2 "To lie" matches "spin a yarn" or "tell a tall tale".

• Option 4 "To be caught stealing" matches "be caught red-handed".

NOTE

• Related idioms of hard work: "burn the midnight oil" (study/work late), "put one's shoulder to the wheel", "sweat blood", "leave no stone unturned".

• The negative form "without breaking a sweat" means "very easily, with no effort at all".

question:
Select the appropriate antonym for the underlined word.

There can’t be anything positive about plastics with pathogens floating around.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. depreciative.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Positive" here means favourable, approving, expressing support or praise. Its antonym is "depreciative", meaning expressing disapproval or criticism; belittling the value of something. (निंदात्मक / अवमूल्यन करने वाला)

◦ Example: Her positive remarks encouraged him, while his depreciative comments discouraged the team.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "approving" (showing agreement/praise) is a synonym of positive, not an antonym.

• Option 2 "flattering" (praising excessively) is also close in sense to positive.

• Option 4 "fundamental" means basic or essential — it is unrelated to the positive/negative axis.

NOTE

• Synonyms of positive: affirmative, optimistic, favourable, constructive.

• Antonyms of positive: negative, depreciative, disparaging, pessimistic, derogatory.

• Note the related words: depreciate (to fall in value / to belittle) vs appreciate (to rise in value / to value highly).

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.

Curtailed
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Lengthened.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Curtailed" means cut short, reduced or shortened in extent or duration. Its antonym is "lengthened", meaning made longer or extended. (छोटा करना का विलोम — लंबा करना)

◦ Example: The programme was curtailed because of rain, but next year it was lengthened to two days.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Slashed" (cut drastically, especially prices/budgets) is a synonym of curtailed.

• Option 3 "Pruned" (cut back branches; trimmed down) is also a synonym.

• Option 4 "Trimmed" (cut off small amounts to neaten/reduce) is likewise a synonym.

• Three options mean "to cut/reduce"; only "lengthened" moves in the opposite direction — a useful elimination strategy in antonym questions.

NOTE

• Synonyms of curtail: cut back, abridge, truncate, diminish, restrict.

• Antonyms of curtail: lengthen, extend, prolong, increase, expand, augment.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

This is most unique thing I have ever seen in my life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. This is most unique.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• There are two faults packed into this segment:

◦ "Unique" is an absolute (non-gradable) adjective — something is either unique or it is not. It therefore cannot take "more/most/very".

◦ Even if a superlative were allowed, it would need the definite article "the" before it ("the most ..."), which is missing.

• The natural correction is to drop "most" and use the article "the":

◦ Correct: This is the most unusual/the only unique thing I have ever seen in my life — or simply, This is a unique thing I have ever seen in my life.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "thing I have ever" is correct; "ever" is regularly used with the present perfect in such superlative-type structures.

• Option 3 "seen in my life." is correct — "seen" is the proper past participle after "have".

• Option 1 "No error" is ruled out by the faulty use of "most unique".

NOTE

• Other absolute adjectives that take no comparative/superlative: perfect, complete, universal, entire, extreme, supreme, ideal, eternal, chief, final, round, square, empty, full.

• Rule: a superlative in English normally requires "the" — "the tallest boy", "the most beautiful painting".

question:
Select the appropriate synonym for the underlined word.

It is not that you seem heartless.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. cruel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Heartless" means completely lacking pity or compassion; unfeeling and hard-hearted. Its closest synonym among the options is "cruel". (निर्दयी / निष्ठुर)

◦ Example: It was heartless/cruel of him to abandon the injured puppy.

• The suffix "-less" means "without": heart + less = "without heart", i.e., without feeling.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "robust" means strong and healthy (हृष्ट-पुष्ट) — unrelated to feeling.

• Option 2 "warm" (affectionate, kind-hearted) is an antonym of heartless.

• Option 3 "mild" (gentle, not severe) is also opposite in tone.

NOTE

• Synonyms of heartless: cruel, callous, merciless, ruthless, pitiless, unfeeling, stony-hearted.

• Antonyms of heartless: kind, compassionate, warm, humane, merciful, tender-hearted.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘no substitution required’.

No, they are normal people, (although they perceive the world different).
option_1: but they perceive the world differently
option_3: from they perceive the world differently
option_4: while they perceive the world different
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. but they perceive the world differently.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Two corrections are needed in the bracketed segment:

◦ "different" is an adjective, but the word modifies the verb "perceive", so the adverb "differently" is required.

◦ The sentence contrasts two ideas ("they are normal people" vs "they see things in another way"); the coordinating conjunction "but" joins them naturally and idiomatically here.

◦ Correct: No, they are normal people, but they perceive the world differently.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "No substitution required" is wrong because "perceive ... different" is grammatically incorrect.

• Option 3 "from they perceive ..." is meaningless — "from" is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause like this.

• Option 4 "while they perceive the world different" still keeps the wrong adjective "different" instead of "differently".

NOTE

• Adjectives modify nouns/pronouns (a different view); adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs (they see it differently).

• Most adverbs of manner are formed by adding "-ly": quick → quickly, different → differently, careful → carefully.

question: Four sentences are given, out of which three have spelling errors. Choose the sentence with all correctly spelt words.
option_1: He made the most delicious pumkin pie.
option_2: The paralel lives of two contemporaries.
option_3: She took a pair of sissors and cut his hair.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I need a strong adhesive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 4 is spelt correctly. "Adhesive" means a substance such as glue used for sticking things together. (चिपकाने वाला पदार्थ)

• Spelling key: AD + HE + SIVE (from the verb "adhere" — to stick to).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "pumkin" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "pumpkin" (with a "p" after "pum").

• Option 2: "paralel" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "parallel" (one "r", double "l" in the middle: PAR + AL + LEL).

• Option 3: "sissors" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "scissors" (silent "c": SC + IS + SORS).

NOTE

• Frequently misspelt SSC words worth memorising: parallel, scissors, pumpkin, occurrence, embarrass, questionnaire, maintenance, privilege, receive, separate, definitely.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

He started a newly jobs on Tuesday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. a new job.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined part contains two errors:

◦ "newly" is an adverb; the word qualifies the noun "job(s)", so the adjective "new" is needed.

◦ The article "a" is singular, so the noun must also be singular — "job", not "jobs".

• Hence the correct phrase is "a new job".

◦ Correct: He started a new job on Tuesday.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "No improvement" is wrong because "a newly jobs" is doubly incorrect.

• Option 3 "a new jobs" keeps the article–noun disagreement (a + plural noun).

• Option 4 "an new job" uses "an" before the consonant sound /n/ — "an" is used only before a vowel sound.

NOTE

• Article rule: "a" before a consonant sound (a job, a university, a one-rupee coin); "an" before a vowel sound (an hour, an MP, an apple).

• Adjective vs adverb: "a new job" (adjective + noun) but "a newly built house" (adverb + participle).

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To poke one’s nose into
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To interfere.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to poke one's nose into (something)" means to interfere or meddle in other people's affairs without being asked. (दूसरों के मामलों में दखल देना / टाँग अड़ाना)

◦ Example: Stop poking your nose into my family matters.

• The image is of pushing one's nose where it does not belong — hence unwanted intrusion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "To give permission" would be "give the green light" or "give the go-ahead".

• Option 2 "To show disrespect" would be "look down upon" or "turn up one's nose at".

• Option 3 "To bring no sense" does not correspond to any standard idiom.

NOTE

• Related "nose" idioms: "lead someone by the nose" (control completely), "turn up one's nose at" (reject scornfully), "keep one's nose clean" (stay out of trouble), "pay through the nose" (pay far too much).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

I strained ______ to catch his options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. hard.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hard" is used here as an adverb of manner meaning with great effort/intensely, and it modifies the verb "strained".

◦ Correct: I strained hard to catch his options.

• "Hard" is one of those words whose adverb form is identical to the adjective (a hard task / to work hard). No "-ly" is added.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "hardly" is a negative adverb meaning "scarcely/almost not". "I strained hardly" would absurdly mean "I hardly strained".

• Option 3 "hardest" is the superlative and would need a comparison group plus usually "the".

• Option 4 "hardness" is a noun and cannot modify a verb.

NOTE

• Adverbs with two forms and different meanings: hard (with effort) / hardly (scarcely); late (not early) / lately (recently); near (close) / nearly (almost); high (at a height) / highly (very much).

• "Hardly, scarcely, barely" are negative in sense, so they are never used with another negative word.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

Rohan was now standing on tiptoe to ______ over at the inhabitants of the two beds.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. look.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb needed must fit the prepositional pattern "______ over at". The natural, idiomatic combination in English is "look over at (somebody)", meaning to direct one's eyes towards someone a little distance away. (नज़र डालना)

◦ Correct: Rohan was now standing on tiptoe to look over at the inhabitants of the two beds.

• "Standing on tiptoe" signals that he is stretching up merely to see across — exactly the casual sense of "look over at".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "view" is a transitive verb taking a direct object ("view the scene"); "view over at" is not an English collocation.

• Option 3 "stare" means to gaze fixedly and takes "stare at", not "stare over at".

• Option 4 "peep" means to look quickly and secretly, usually "peep through/into" a small opening — it does not take "over at".

NOTE

• Verbs of seeing and their prepositions: look at / look over at / look into, stare at, glance at, peep through, gaze upon, glare at.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of people who have no permanent abode but wander from place to place
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Nomad.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "nomad" is a member of a community that has no fixed home and moves from place to place, usually in search of pasture, water or food. (घुमंतू / खानाबदोश)

◦ Example: The nomads of Central Asia migrate with their herds every season.

• The adjective form is "nomadic" and the way of life is called "nomadism".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Truant" — a pupil who stays away from school without permission.

• Option 3 "Ponderer" — one who thinks deeply about something.

• Option 4 "Usurer" — one who lends money at an unreasonably high rate of interest (सूदखोर).

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: vagabond/vagrant (a wanderer with no settled home or work), itinerant (travelling from place to place for work), emigrant (one who leaves his own country), immigrant (one who comes into a foreign country to settle).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Artiset.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Artiset" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "artist", meaning a person who creates art — paintings, sculpture, music or other creative work. (कलाकार)

• Spelling key: ART + IST. The suffix "-ist" denotes a person who practises something: artist, scientist, dentist, novelist, pianist.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "Banker" (a person who manages or owns a bank), "Robber" (a person who steals using force or threat) and "Teacher" (a person who teaches) are all correctly spelt.

• Note that these three use the agent suffix "-er", while "artist" uses "-ist" — mixing the two is the trap here.

NOTE

• Distinguish the near-look-alikes: artist (a creator of art), artiste (a professional performer such as a singer or dancer), and artisan (a skilled manual worker/craftsman).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Plastic inhabits the oceans, ______ up in the guts of seagulls and great white sharks.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. building.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "build up" means to accumulate/collect gradually in increasing quantity. Plastic waste gradually accumulates inside the digestive tracts of sea creatures, so "building up in the guts of seagulls and great white sharks" is the intended sense. (जमा होना / इकट्ठा होना)

◦ Correct: Plastic inhabits the oceans, building up in the guts of seagulls and great white sharks.

• The participle "building" also correctly forms a participial phrase describing what the plastic does.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "burning up" means to be destroyed by fire or to use up energy — plastic does not burn inside a bird's stomach.

• Option 3 "provoking" means to deliberately annoy or incite; it does not take "up" in this sense.

• Option 4 "sailing" means to travel on water by ship — it cannot describe matter collecting inside a gut.

NOTE

• Useful phrasal verbs with "up": build up (accumulate), bring up (raise/mention), give up (quit), take up (start a hobby), put up with (tolerate), turn up (arrive).

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

That can be carried or moved easily
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Portable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Portable" means able to be easily carried or moved, especially because it is light in weight. (सुवाह्य / आसानी से ले जाने योग्य)

◦ Example: A portable speaker can be carried in a bag.

• It comes from the Latin "portare" = to carry (the same root gives us port, porter, transport, export, import).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Illegible" — writing that cannot be read (अपठनीय).

• Option 2 "Handful" — a small quantity that fills the hand, or a troublesome person.

• Option 4 "Potable" — fit to drink (पीने योग्य). "Potable water" means drinking water. Note the near-identical look of portable and potable — a classic SSC trap.

NOTE

• Adjectives ending in "-able/-ible" as one-word substitutes: audible (that can be heard), edible (fit to eat), legible (that can be read), inevitable (that cannot be avoided), incorrigible (that cannot be corrected).

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

A young man walks toward me with a stick slung across his back and a (1)______ of sheep at his feet, which carry him down the path (2)______ a crowd of rowdy children. An older man follows, weatherworn but still (3)______, a rifle over his left shoulder. He clicks his tongue to (4)______ the flock. Behind him are two women on horses; I guess (5)______ are his wife and daughter.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. flock.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct collective noun for sheep is a "flock of sheep". (भेड़ों का झुंड)

◦ Correct: ... a stick slung across his back and a flock of sheep at his feet ...

• The passage itself confirms this later: "He clicks his tongue to ______ the flock" — the same word is used for the same group of animals.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "army" is used for soldiers or ants (an army of ants).

• Option 2 "shoal" is used for fish (a shoal of fish).

• Option 3 "horde" suggests a large, disorderly crowd of people, not domestic animals.

NOTE

• Common collective nouns: a flock of sheep/birds, a herd of cattle/elephants, a pack of wolves, a swarm of bees, a pride of lions, a school/shoal of fish, a litter of puppies, a gaggle of geese.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

A young man walks toward me with a stick slung across his back and a (1)______ of sheep at his feet, which carry him down the path (2)______ a crowd of rowdy children. An older man follows, weatherworn but still (3)______, a rifle over his left shoulder. He clicks his tongue to (4)______ the flock. Behind him are two women on horses; I guess (5)______ are his wife and daughter.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. like.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Here the blank needs a preposition of comparison. "Like" means "similar to / in the manner of" and is followed directly by a noun phrase — here, "a crowd of rowdy children".

◦ Correct: ... which carry him down the path like a crowd of rowdy children.

• The comparison is vivid: the milling sheep bustle around him just as a noisy crowd of children would.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "likeness" is a noun meaning resemblance — a noun cannot link the clause to the following noun phrase.

• Option 3 "likely" is an adjective/adverb meaning "probable/probably" and does not express comparison.

• Option 4 "liking" is a noun meaning fondness ("a liking for sweets").

NOTE

• "Like" (preposition) is followed by a noun/pronoun: "He runs like a deer."

• "As" (conjunction) is followed by a clause with a verb: "He runs as a deer runs."

• "As" is also used to mean "in the capacity of": "She works as a teacher."

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

A young man walks toward me with a stick slung across his back and a (1)______ of sheep at his feet, which carry him down the path (2)______ a crowd of rowdy children. An older man follows, weatherworn but still (3)______, a rifle over his left shoulder. He clicks his tongue to (4)______ the flock. Behind him are two women on horses; I guess (5)______ are his wife and daughter.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. strong.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The key word is the contrastive conjunction "but still". The older man is described as "weatherworn" (worn and aged by exposure to sun, wind and rain), and the contrast that follows must be a positive quality — he is aged in appearance but still strong. (फिर भी मज़बूत)

◦ Correct: An older man follows, weatherworn but still strong, a rifle over his left shoulder.

• The detail of a rifle carried over his shoulder while walking supports the sense of continuing physical strength.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Options 2 "sick", 3 "thin" and 4 "slow" are all negative/weakening descriptions. Placing any of them after "but still" destroys the contrast, because "weatherworn" is already negative.

NOTE

• Contrast markers such as but, yet, still, although, though, however, nevertheless, in spite of always signal that the idea after them opposes the idea before them. Spotting them is the fastest way to solve cloze questions.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

A young man walks toward me with a stick slung across his back and a (1)______ of sheep at his feet, which carry him down the path (2)______ a crowd of rowdy children. An older man follows, weatherworn but still (3)______, a rifle over his left shoulder. He clicks his tongue to (4)______ the flock. Behind him are two women on horses; I guess (5)______ are his wife and daughter.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. encourage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A shepherd clicks his tongue as a signal to urge his animals along. "Encourage" means to urge on, to give support or confidence so that someone/something keeps going, which is exactly what the clicking sound does to the flock. (प्रोत्साहित करना / हाँकना)

◦ Correct: He clicks his tongue to encourage the flock.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "punish" (to penalise for wrongdoing) makes no sense — a click of the tongue punishes nothing.

• Option 2 "claim" (to demand as one's right) is unrelated to driving animals.

• Option 4 "dress" (to put clothes on) is absurd in the context of sheep.

NOTE

• Verb + object collocations for herding: drive the flock, urge on the herd, round up the cattle, herd the sheep, encourage the animals forward.

question:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

A young man walks toward me with a stick slung across his back and a (1)______ of sheep at his feet, which carry him down the path (2)______ a crowd of rowdy children. An older man follows, weatherworn but still (3)______, a rifle over his left shoulder. He clicks his tongue to (4)______ the flock. Behind him are two women on horses; I guess (5)______ are his wife and daughter.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. they.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is the subject of the verb "are" in the noun clause "I guess (that) ______ are his wife and daughter". A subject pronoun referring to two women is required, so the third-person plural subject pronoun "they" is correct.

◦ Correct: Behind him are two women on horses; I guess they are his wife and daughter.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "them" is an object pronoun and cannot be the subject of "are".

• Option 2 "these" is a demonstrative used for things/people near the speaker; the women are at a distance behind the man, and "they" is the natural anaphoric reference.

• Option 4 "this" is singular and cannot agree with the plural verb "are" or refer to two women.

NOTE

• Subject pronouns: I, we, you, he, she, it, they. Object pronouns: me, us, you, him, her, it, them.

• Demonstratives: this/these (near), that/those (far); this/that are singular, these/those are plural.
